items.text: Under Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, what is the primary task of statutory interpretation?
To discern and give effect to the intent of the Legislature. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
According to Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, what is the most reliable evidence of the Legislature's intent?
The words of the statute itself. The statutory text is the most reliable evidence of legislative intent. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
If a Michigan statute's language is unambiguous, what does Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward say a court must do?
Enforce it as written. No further judicial construction is required or permitted. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
Under Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, when may a court go beyond the words of a statute to look for intent elsewhere?
Only where the statutory language is ambiguous. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
What grammatical canon did Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward itself apply to find a statute unambiguous?
The last-antecedent rule: a modifying word or clause attaches only to the term right before it, not to everything earlier in the sentence. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
What does the in pari materia canon mean, and which Michigan case states it?

Statutes on the same subject or sharing a common purpose are read together as one law. A statute must be read in conjunction with other relevant statutes to ascertain legislative intent. Potter v McLeary, 484 Mich 397 (2009).
In Potter v McLeary, how does the Michigan Supreme Court describe reading a statute's words and phrases?
They should be read in the context of the entire legislative scheme, so the statute works in harmony with the entire statutory scheme. Potter v McLeary, 484 Mich 397 (2009).
What is the classic, older Michigan statement of the in pari materia rule, and which case gives it?

All statutes relating to the same subject, or having the same general purpose, should be read in connection with it, as together constituting one law. City of Detroit v Michigan Bell Telephone Co, 374 Mich 543, 558 (1965).
TRAP: Does the in pari materia canon require a finding of ambiguity before a Michigan court can use it?

No, not strictly. The Michigan Supreme Court has said its application is not necessarily conditioned on a finding of ambiguity. It is the one canon in this chapter that does not always wait for ambiguity. SBC Health Midwest, Inc v City of Kentwood, 500 Mich 65, 73 n 26 (2017).
Even though in pari materia can apply without ambiguity, what can it never do to an unambiguous statute?

A court may read nothing into an unambiguous statute that is not within the manifest intent of the Legislature. In pari materia can inform context, but it cannot override or narrow clear text. SBC Health Midwest, Inc v City of Kentwood, 500 Mich 65, 73 n 26 (2017).
What does the ejusdem generis canon mean, and which Michigan case applies it?

When a statute lists specific items and adds a general catch-all phrase, the catch-all is limited to things of the same kind as the specific list. The meaning of the general words is ordinarily restricted by the particular designation. People v Smith, 393 Mich 432 (1975).
In People v Smith, a concealed-weapons statute listed 'dagger, dirk, stiletto' plus a general catch-all. Why didn't a thirty-inch rifle fall under the catch-all?

Ejusdem generis limited the catch-all to other stabbing weapons of the same kind as the specific list, so a rifle (a different kind of weapon, separately addressed by the statute) did not qualify. People v Smith, 393 Mich 432 (1975).
What does the noscitur a sociis canon mean, and which Michigan case states it?

A word's meaning is shaped by the words sitting next to it. A word or phrase is known from its associates and is given meaning by its context or setting. Tyler v Livonia Pub Schools, 459 Mich 382 (1999).
What is the difference between in pari materia and noscitur a sociis?

In pari materia reads whole related statutes together to find a shared meaning. Noscitur a sociis is narrower: it reads one word against the specific words immediately next to it in the same sentence or list.
What does expressio unius est exclusio alterius mean, and which Michigan case applies it?

When the Legislature writes a specific list, things not on the list are presumed left out on purpose. The expression of one thing suggests the exclusion of all others. Michigan Gun Owners, Inc v Ann Arbor Pub Schools, 502 Mich 695 (2018).
A Michigan preemption statute named cities, villages, townships, and counties, but not school districts. Under Michigan Gun Owners, Inc v Ann Arbor Pub Schools, what does that omission mean?

Under expressio unius est exclusio alterius, naming specific local units and leaving school districts off the list means school districts were not covered by the preemption, so they could adopt their own firearms policies. Michigan Gun Owners, Inc v Ann Arbor Pub Schools, 502 Mich 695 (2018).
Michigan Gun Owners, Inc v Ann Arbor Pub Schools quotes the expressio unius maxim from which earlier Michigan Supreme Court case?
People v Wilson, 500 Mich 521, 526 (2017): "the expression of one thing suggests the exclusion of all others." Michigan Gun Owners, Inc v Ann Arbor Pub Schools, 502 Mich 695 (2018).
Under In re Certified Question, when is it proper for a Michigan court to resort to legislative history?
Only where a genuine ambiguity exists in the statute. Resort to legislative history of any form is proper only in that circumstance. In re Certified Question, 468 Mich 109 (2003).
A statute's text is clear, but a contractor wants to argue a committee report shows the Legislature really meant something broader. Does Michigan law let a court consider that report?

No. Under In re Certified Question, resort to legislative history is proper only where a genuine ambiguity exists in the statute. Clear text ends the inquiry. In re Certified Question, 468 Mich 109 (2003).
How does contra proferentem's place in Klapp's sequence mirror the statutory canons covered in this chapter?

Both share the same architecture: read the text first, use interpretive tools only if genuinely ambiguous, and only at the very end apply a tie-breaking presumption. Klapp treats contra proferentem as a last-resort tie-breaker, the contract-law twin of the statutory canons. Klapp v United Ins Group Agency, Inc, 468 Mich 459 (2003).
Does finding a statute or policy ambiguous automatically mean the insured or the party favored by the ambiguity wins?

No. Under both the statutory canons and Klapp's contra proferentem sequence, ambiguity opens the door to context and extrinsic evidence first. Only if those tools still leave the question unresolved does a tie-breaking presumption apply.
Under Rovas, how much weight does a court give a state agency's own interpretation of a statute it administers?

Respectful consideration, but the agency's interpretation is not binding on the courts and cannot conflict with the Legislature's intent. In re Complaint of Rovas Against SBC Michigan, 482 Mich 90 (2008).
What did Rovas say about courts deferring entirely to an administrative agency's reading of a statute?
Courts may not abdicate to administrative agencies the constitutional responsibility to construe statutes. In re Complaint of Rovas Against SBC Michigan, 482 Mich 90 (2008).
A carrier's claims position rests only on the wording of a DIFS bulletin, with no statutory text backing it up. How strong is that position in court, under Rovas?

Weaker than it looks. A DIFS bulletin gets respectful consideration but is not binding on a court, and cannot conflict with the Legislature's actual intent. A position rooted in the statute's own text is much harder to dislodge. In re Complaint of Rovas Against SBC Michigan, 482 Mich 90 (2008).
Besides not being binding on courts, what else can happen to a DIFS bulletin that cannot happen to a statute?

DIFS can reissue or withdraw a bulletin on its own, with no legislative vote required. A statute changes only through the legislative process. This is the same instrument hierarchy covered in Domain 01, applied here to how hard you can argue each one.
DIFS Bulletin 2026-16-INS announces the current MCL 500.2227 fire-insurance maximum-withholding figure as $25,090. Is that number independently binding law because DIFS published it?

No. The bulletin is DIFS doing the statute's own CPI-indexed math and announcing the result. The governing authority is MCL 500.2227's formula. If DIFS miscalculated, the statute's formula controls, not the bulletin's printed number.
What is a Michigan Judicial Institute (MJI) benchbook, and why start research there instead of a raw case search?

An MJI benchbook is a public, subject-organized reference written for Michigan judges, published on courts.michigan.gov. It gets you oriented fast with citations already attached, organized the way a judge actually thinks through the problem, before you pull the underlying statute or case text yourself.
What are the three steps of the Michigan legal-research workflow for a statutory question, in order?

Start with the relevant MJI benchbook to get oriented and find the controlling cases. Then pull the actual statutory text yourself from legislature.mi.gov rather than trusting a paraphrase. Then confirm any case you plan to rely on is still good law and has not been narrowed or overruled.
What judge-made rule did Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co create for Michigan fire-policy suit deadlines?

It tolled (paused) the running of a policy's one-year suit deadline from the time the insured gives notice of loss until the insurer formally denies liability. Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co, 396 Mich 588 (1976).
How did Rory v Continental Ins Co partially overrule Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co?

Rory overruled Tom Thomas, Camelot, and their progeny only to the degree they abrogated unambiguous contractual terms on the basis of reasonableness determinations. Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005).
After Rory, does Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co's tolling holding still survive?

Yes. Rory only killed Tom Thomas's reasonableness rationale, not its tolling holding. The tolling rule survives and is now written directly into statute at MCL 500.2833(1)(q). Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co, 396 Mich 588 (1976); Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005).
Someone cites Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co for the proposition that one-year contractual suit deadlines are unreasonable and unenforceable. What is wrong with that citation?

That is citing the half of Tom Thomas that Rory overruled. Rory killed only the reasonableness rationale; the tolling holding is the half that survives. Citing Tom Thomas for 'unreasonable deadlines are unenforceable' cites dead law. Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005).
What is the general research lesson Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co and Rory v Continental Ins Co together teach?

Good law can become dead law without being formally repealed, because a later case narrows or overrules part of an earlier holding. Always confirm a case is still good law, and check which specific piece of its holding you are relying on, before citing it.
What is the Michigan textualist practitioner move for arguing any coverage or statutory question?

Find the actual text that answers the question and argue that first. Only reach for a canon, extrinsic evidence, or a fairness argument once you can show the text is genuinely ambiguous. Michigan courts are required to decide the case that way; see Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
Why is 'that's not fair' almost never a winning legal argument in a Michigan coverage or statutory dispute?

Both the statutory side (Sun Valley: unambiguous text is enforced as written, no further judicial construction) and the contract side (Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005): judicial reasonableness is an invalid basis to refuse to enforce unambiguous terms) reject fairness as a basis to override clear language. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999); Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005).
What does it mean for a statute or contract term to be 'ambiguous' under Michigan law?
Its provisions are capable of conflicting interpretations, or two clauses in the same document irreconcilably conflict. A debatable or hard question is not automatically an ambiguous one.
Why doesn't Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward itself discuss in pari materia or legislative history?

Because the Court resolved the case using the plain text and the last-antecedent grammatical canon, finding no ambiguity. It never needed to reach the other canons. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).

A fire-policy exclusion reads: 'loss caused by flood, surface water, waves, tidal water, or overflow of a body of water, whether driven by wind or not.' A homeowner argues 'whether driven by wind or not' modifies only 'overflow of a body of water,' so wind-driven rain elsewhere is covered. What canon governs this argument?

The last-antecedent rule: a modifying phrase attaches only to the term immediately before it, not to everything earlier in the list. A court applies that grammatical reading before ever reaching ambiguity or fairness arguments.

A policy excludes loss from 'termites, carpenter ants, beetles, or other insects or vermin.' A carrier tries to deny an unrelated contamination claim by calling it 'vermin.' What canon limits that argument?
Ejusdem generis. The general word 'vermin' following a specific list of wood-destroying pests is limited to things of that same kind, not any unrelated contamination issue.
What is Michigan district court's exclusive civil jurisdiction ceiling, and what does that ceiling actually control?

$25,000. MCL 600.8301(1): the district court has exclusive jurisdiction in civil actions when the amount in controversy does not exceed $25,000. It determines which court can hear the case at all, not a damages cap or a filing-fee rule.
A homeowner's water-damage dispute is worth about $22,000. Which Michigan court has exclusive jurisdiction, and what does that mean for cost?
District court, under MCL 600.8301(1)'s $25,000 ceiling. District court has a faster docket and simpler procedure than circuit court, so the fight is typically cheaper for both sides.
A homeowner's fire claim is worth $90,000 and the carrier is contesting coverage hard. Which court does this land in, and what does that change about the fight?

Circuit court, because it is above the MCL 600.8301(1) $25,000 ceiling. Circuit court means heavier discovery, a full jury-trial right if demanded within 28 days of the answer, and a more expensive fight for both sides, which raises the leverage of whichever party can outlast the cost.
Why would a carrier sometimes fight hard over coverage on a claim sitting right around the $25,000 district-court ceiling?

Pushing the dispute into circuit court (above MCL 600.8301(1)'s ceiling) raises the cost of litigating for both sides. Raised cost is leverage against whichever side has less time or money to spend on the fight.
Below district court's general civil jurisdiction, what narrower division handles Michigan claims up to $7,000, and what is unusual about it?
Small claims, under MCL 600.8401. Unlike ordinary district court cases, attorneys generally cannot take part in filing, prosecuting, or defending a small claims case except on their own behalf.
What is the standard of review a Michigan appellate court applies to a lower court's statutory interpretation?
De novo. The appellate court reviews the interpretation fresh, without deferring to the lower court's reading.
Name the four canons covered in this chapter that Michigan courts reach for once a statute is found ambiguous.
In pari materia, ejusdem generis, noscitur a sociis, and expressio unius est exclusio alterius. Legislative history is a fifth, last-resort tool, usable only on a genuine ambiguity.
You are researching whether a specific Michigan Chapter 12 adjuster-licensing provision applies to a given fact pattern. What should you check first, before pulling case law?

Start with the relevant MJI benchbook (if one covers the topic) to get oriented, then pull the actual statutory text from legislature.mi.gov yourself, then confirm any case you plan to rely on is still good law.
What does it mean to say a case can be 'good law' on one point and 'dead law' on another at the same time?

A later case can overrule part of an earlier holding while leaving the rest intact. Tom Thomas Organization, Inc v Reliance Ins Co, 396 Mich 588 (1976) is the worked example: its reasonableness rationale is dead (overruled by Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005)), but its tolling holding is still good law and is now codified at MCL 500.2833(1)(q).
What is the key difference between how hard you can argue a position built on a DIFS bulletin versus one built on the statute the bulletin interprets?

A bulletin-only position is persuasive and useful for settlement leverage, but a court is free to disagree with it, and DIFS can rewrite or withdraw it without a legislative vote. A statute-based position is much harder to dislodge because changing it requires an actual legislative amendment.
Circuit court sits above district court in Michigan's trial-level structure. What is circuit court's general jurisdiction?

Circuit court has original jurisdiction to hear and determine all civil claims and remedies except where exclusive jurisdiction is given to some other court, plus felonies, and appeals from district and probate court.
What kind of review does the Michigan Court of Appeals have over a circuit-court final judgment, and what kind does the Michigan Supreme Court have over the Court of Appeals?

The Court of Appeals has jurisdiction as of right over final judgments and final orders from circuit court, the Court of Claims, and probate court. The Michigan Supreme Court reviews only by discretionary leave to appeal.

A restoration contractor wants to cite a DIFS bulletin as though it settles a coverage dispute on its own, with no statutory text behind it. What is the accurate way to frame that argument to a court?

Frame it as what DIFS currently believes the statute means, entitled to respectful consideration, not as binding law. Pair it with the statute's own text wherever possible, because the text is what actually controls if the two conflict.
What is the single biggest practical tell, from Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, for how Michigan courts actually decide statutory questions?

Text first, and most of the time the text alone is enough. Sun Valley resolved its own case with plain text and a grammatical canon, never needing ambiguity-stage tools like in pari materia or legislative history. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
List, in order, the four-step Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward framework for reading any Michigan statute.

One, legislative intent is the goal. Two, the statutory text is the most reliable evidence of that intent. Three, unambiguous text is enforced as written with no further judicial construction. Four, only ambiguity opens the door to canons, extrinsic evidence, or legislative history. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
A lawyer researching a Michigan insurance-licensing question finds a 1995 Court of Appeals case that looks perfect. Before citing it in a brief, what must the lawyer confirm?

That the case is still good law: that it has not been narrowed, abrogated, or overruled by a later Court of Appeals or Supreme Court opinion, the same way Rory partially overruled Tom Thomas Organization decades after it was decided.
Is 'this seems unfair, so the statute shouldn't apply' a valid legal argument under Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward?

No. If the text is unambiguous, the statute is enforced as written regardless of fairness concerns. Fairness only becomes relevant, if ever, through a recognized legal doctrine, not as a freestanding override of clear text. Sun Valley Foods Co v Ward, 460 Mich 230 (1999).
